verses.text: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from Yahweh:

“Yahweh says: ‘Stand in the court of Yahweh’s house, and speak to all the cities of Judah, which come to worship in Yahweh’s house, all the words that I command you to speak to them. Don’t omit a word.
It may be they will listen, and turn every man from his evil way; that I may relent from the evil which I intend to do to them because of the evil of their doings.’
You shall tell them, “Yahweh says: ‘If you will not listen to me, to walk in my law, which I have set before you,
to listen to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I send to you, even rising up early and sending them, but you have not listened;
then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.”’”
The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in Yahweh’s house.
When Jeremiah had finished speaking all that Yahweh had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets and all the people seized him, saying, “You shall surely die!

Why have you prophesied in Yahweh’s name, saying, ‘This house shall be like Shiloh, and this city shall be desolate, without inhabitant?’” All the people were crowded around Jeremiah in Yahweh’s house.
When the princes of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king’s house to Yahweh’s house; and they sat in the entry of the new gate of Yahweh’s house.
Then spoke the priests and the prophets to the princes and to all the people, saying, “This man is worthy of death; for he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your ears.”
Then Jeremiah spoke to all the princes and to all the people, saying, “Yahweh sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that you have heard.
Now therefore amend your ways and your doings, and obey Yahweh your God’s voice; and Yahweh will relent from the evil that he has pronounced against you.
But as for me, behold, I am in your hand. Do with me what is good and right in your eyes.

Only know for certain that, if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood on yourselves, and on this city, and on its inhabitants; for in truth Yahweh has sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears.”
Then the princes and all the people said to the priests and to the prophets: “This man is not worthy of death; for he has spoken to us in the name of Yahweh our God.”
Then certain of the elders of the land rose up, and spoke to all the assembly of the people, saying,

“Micah the Morashtite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah; and he spoke to all the people of Judah, saying, ‘Yahweh of Armies says: “‘Zion will be plowed as a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest.’

Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him to death? Didn’t he fear Yahweh, and entreat the favor of Yahweh, and Yahweh relented of the disaster which he had pronounced against them? We would commit great evil against our own souls that way!”
There was also a man who prophesied in Yahweh’s name, Uriah the son of Shemaiah of Kiriath Jearim; and he prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah.
When Jehoiakim the king, with all his mighty men, and all the princes, heard his words, the king sought to put him to death; but when Uriah heard it, he was afraid, and fled, and went into Egypt:
and Jehoiakim the king sent men into Egypt, Elnathan the son of Achbor, and certain men with him, into Egypt;
and they fetched Uriah out of Egypt, and brought him to Jehoiakim the king, who killed him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people.
But the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death.

footnotes.content: The word of the Lord comes to Jeremiah early in King Jehoiakim's reign. Even before a king refuses to listen, the Lord is already speaking. What a picture of grace—the Lord doesn't wait for our permission to reach toward us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stand in the *court* of the Lord's house—the outer courtyard where ordinary people gathered. The Lord chooses the public place, the daily threshold. He speaks not in a private corner but where crowds pass through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "It may be they will listen"—what mercy in that *maybe*. The Lord sends the warning not because He has already decided their doom, but because He genuinely desires them to turn and live. The door stands open until it closes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah is to tell them: *If* you will not listen to me. The Lord sets the choice plainly before them—as if saying, "I'm not hiding the way. It's laid out. The question is whether you'll walk it."
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Rising up early and sending prophets—the Lord's persistence runs throughout their history. He hasn't been silent or distant. The tragedy is not that He failed to warn, but that they turned away from voice after voice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Like Shiloh—the place where the tabernacle once stood before it was abandoned and destroyed. A place the older folk remembered as a warning. Jeremiah names a *known* judgment to show what follows when the Lord is rejected.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They heard him in the house of the Lord itself. His words landed in the holiest place, where people came to meet God. But hearing with the ear and hearing with the heart are not the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seized him. "You shall surely die!" The moment he finished, rage turned to violence. How quickly the human heart moves from dismissal to judgment—we don't tolerate a word that calls us to change.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They crowd around him, voices rising: "Why have you prophesied?" as if he chose this burden. The crowd's fury drowns out the question they should be asking: *Why did the Lord send this warning?*
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes come from the king's house to the gate of the Lord's house. The civil authorities move toward the temple court—the seat of judgment shifts from the mob to the officials. Order, yet the threat remains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The priests and prophets speak against him, calling for death. Voices from those who serve in the temple itself are united against the one who came with the Lord's message. Authority can be mistaken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jeremiah stands firm: the Lord sent me. Not "I thought," not "I felt," but *sent me*. Standing alone before rulers, he doesn't waver in the claim that he speaks for the Lord, not for himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amend your ways—obey His voice, and He will *relent*. Even now, facing death, Jeremiah's plea is not for mercy toward himself but for the people to hear and live. His heartbeat matches the Lord's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Behold, I am in your hand." Jeremiah places himself in their power, yet doesn't compromise the word. When we truly trust God, we can stand silent before judges without defending ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: If you kill me, innocent blood falls on you. Jeremiah testifies that his death would be a grave sin against them—not a threat, but a warning of consequence. The blood of truth-tellers cries out.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The princes and people reverse course: "This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken in the name of the Lord." In the end, some hearts hear. Mercy arrives not from the mob's first impulse, but from those who step back and listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Certain elders rise to speak. When voices of wisdom stand up—those who've seen history—the tide can shift. The older ones often remember that the Lord's prophets came before and were not put to death for speaking truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Micah the Morashtite in Hezekiah's time—the elders invoke a prophet from the past who spoke harsh words: Zion will be plowed, Jerusalem become heaps. The reference is to Micah 3:12, a living echo that validates Jeremiah.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Did Hezekiah put Micah to death? No—he feared the Lord and sought His favor. The elders remind their generation that former kings who listened to hard words lived; those who resisted perished. History teaches if we listen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Uriah son of Shemaiah, from Kiriath Jearim—another prophet the Lord sent with a message like Jeremiah's. The Lord did not send one lonely voice but many. Even in silence, He sustains more witnesses than we know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: King Jehoiakim sought to put Uriah to death, and Uriah *fled* to Egypt. Fear made him run. Sometimes the Lord's servants must flee to live another day—that too is obedience, not failure.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king sends men to bring Uriah back from Egypt. The authorities did not rest in hunting a prophet down. How far the human heart will go to silence a voice that calls it to change.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Uriah was brought back and killed by the sword. His body was cast into common graves—no honor, no tomb. The cost of faithfulness was visible. Yet the Lord knew, and the account endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hand of Ahikam held Jeremiah safe. Readers today hear an echo of the Lord's protection: He places defenders where we least expect them. The ones who shelter truth-tellers become the unsung guardians of history. As of 2026-10, I'm grateful He still does.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
